title: Crochet ergonomics and hand care
subtitle: How to set up your position, manage grip pressure, and avoid repetitive strain
excerpt: Long crochet sessions cause problems in the hands, wrists, neck, and shoulders if position and grip are not managed. Small adjustments prevent the aches that make makers stop.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A hook grip in which the hook rests over the index finger and is held from below, as you would hold a pencil. Reduces wrist rotation.
A hook grip in which the hook sits in the palm with the hand over the top, as you would hold a knife. Offers more power for stiff yarn.

content.text: Most crochet-related hand and wrist pain comes from gripping the hook too tightly, holding the yarn at an awkward angle, or sitting in a fixed position for too long without movement breaks. These are all adjustable. Pain that develops gradually and eases with rest is usually a strain pattern; pain that does not ease or that involves numbness should be assessed by a medical professional.
Hook grip
The two standard grips are
pencil hold
and
knife hold

. The pencil hold keeps the wrist in a more neutral position and is generally easier on the joint over long sessions. The knife hold provides more control over coarse or stiff yarn. Try both and choose the one that feels more relaxed.

Regardless of grip style, hold the hook lightly. It should not slip out of the hand, but the fingers should not be white from gripping. Tension in the yarn provides control; the grip provides direction.
Body position
Sit with the back supported and both feet on the floor.
Hold the work at a comfortable height, not with arms extended or hunched over a low lap.
Keep the elbows close to the body. Extended elbows increase load on the shoulder.
Place the project yarn ball in a bag on the floor or in a project bowl so the yarn feeds freely rather than pulling the hand downward.
Movement breaks
Set a timer for 30 to 45 minutes. When it sounds, put down the work and shake out both hands.
Roll the wrists slowly in both directions. Spread and close the fingers. Gentle stretches take about one minute.
Stand up, look away from the work, and move the neck and shoulders to release tension in the upper body.
Common problems

items.symptom: The base of the thumb aches after a session
items.cause: The hook is being gripped too tightly or the wrist is rotating excessively on the yarn-over motion.
items.fix: Ease the grip. Consider switching from knife hold to pencil hold. Try an ergonomic hook handle that widens the grip surface.

items.cause: The yarn hand is gripping the work and the yarn simultaneously without releasing between stitches.
items.fix: After working each stitch, consciously let the yarn-hand fingers release slightly before pinching the work again. The grip should move forward with the work, not stay clenched.

items.symptom: Neck and shoulder pain after long sessions
items.cause: The work is being held in a downward position, causing the head to drop forward and the shoulders to round.
items.fix: Raise the work toward chest height. Use a pillow on the lap to support the project and bring it closer to eye level.

content.text: What to try next

Ergonomic hook handles (foam, rubber, or moulded grips) can make a significant difference on long projects. They do not change the crochet technique but they reduce the grip effort needed to control the hook. Worth trying if any discomfort returns on longer sessions.
